blocks.label: B1. THE FOUR CONDITIONALS (to / ba / tara / nara) — 12 items
items: 1 | -tara as guaranteed-temporal, not hypothetical | "Uchi ni kaettara, denwa suru ne." | CQ (Eng): "Which happens first, the call or getting home?" | Wrong ⇒ learner has -tara glossed only as 'if'; will hear scheduled plans as speculation and will fail ~30% of ordinary daily-plan talk.

2 | -tara counterfactual with noni | "Motto hayaku ittara, maniatta noni." | TF: Eng probe "He caught it." same/different | Wrong ⇒ no counterfactual reading; hears regret as report. Highest-cost single misparse in the block.

3 | -ba on i-adjective (-kereba) | "Yasukereba kau kedo." | 2AFC audio: yasukereba / yasukattara — both OK; probe is CQ "Has he bought it?" | Wrong ⇒ adjective conditional stem never formed; predicts total absence of -ba in production.

4 | -ba godan formation off the e-stem | Eng cue "isogu — make it conditional" | PROD, native-reference match ("isogeba") | Wrong ⇒ wk-13 e-stem key did not generalize; check jointly with items 85/88 (potential shares the stem).

5 | -to natural/automatic consequence (directions frame) | "Kono kado o migi ni magaru to, hidari ni eki ga arimasu." | CQ: "What's on the left?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot follow spoken directions, one of the few genuinely obligatory -to genres.

6 | -to MAIN-CLAUSE CONSTRAINT (no request/volition/permission in main clause) | "Kono kusuri o nomu to, nemuku narimasu." vs "*Kono kusuri o nomu to, sugu nete kudasai." | 2AFC aural naturalness — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY, non-gating | Wrong ⇒ -to overgeneralized to English 'if'; predicts producing requests and invitations with -to for years.

7 | -to habitual/iterative past | "Kodomo no koro, natsu ni naru to umi ni itta." | CQ: "Once, or every year?" | Wrong ⇒ single-event reading; breaks all childhood-reminiscence narration, a very common conversational genre.

8 | nara taking up the interlocutor's utterance | A: "Osushi ga tabetai naa." B: "Osushi nara, ii mise shitteru yo." | CQ: "Why did B mention a restaurant?" | Wrong ⇒ nara heard as generic 'if'; misses the given-that-you-said pivot, the dominant real use of nara.

9 | iku nara — subordinate event is LATER | "Ginkoo ni iku nara, kore mo onegai." | SEQ: "Is the errand handed over before or after he gets there?" | Wrong ⇒ core nara ordering failure. Scored jointly with 10 as a pair-consistency check (both right = credit 2; one right = credit 0, because guessing yields one).

10 | ittara — subordinate event is EARLIER | "Ginkoo ni ittara, kore mo onegai." | SEQ, identical probe wording to item 9 | Wrong ⇒ same axis. The 9/10 pair is the single most informative pair in the battery; separate by >=40 items.
11 | -tara mirative / discovery | "Mado o aketara, yuki ga futte ita." | CQ: "Did he expect snow?" | Wrong ⇒ misses the discovery -tara that carries most first-person narration.

12 | Conditional SELECTION under production pressure | Eng situation: "Say: if it rains, the trip is off." | 4AFC audio: furu to / futtara / fureba / furu nara | Wrong ⇒ nara-overuse (the classic English-speaker default) or -to-overuse; diagnoses which of the four is the learner's illegitimate default.
blocks.rationale: Largest block (12) because conditionals combine top-decile conversational frequency with the highest residual error rate at month 9 of anything in the closed set: four forms, overlapping distributions, one hard syntactic constraint (-to), and one ordering contrast (nara/tara) that is invisible in translation. English collapses all four onto 'if/when', so there is no L1 scaffold at all. Error-proneness x frequency puts this above every other category.
blocks.interference: Items 9/10 are a minimal pair and must be >=40 items apart in administration order (put 9 in the first quarter, 10 in the last). Items 1 and 11 both use -tara non-hypothetically and must not be adjacent. Item 4 (-ba off e-stem) shares the e-stem with B10 potential — separate by >=20 items or a correct answer on one inflates the other. Item 3's yasukereba must not follow any B12 adjective item.

blocks.label: B2. -TE AUXILIARIES — 11 items
items: 13 | -teru progressive (contracted citation form) | "Ima gohan tabeteru." | CQ: "Now or later?" | ANCHOR ITEM — near-ceiling expected. A miss here invalidates the session (fatigue, audio, or attention problem); rerun rather than score.

14 | -teru RESULTATIVE state (change-of-state verb) | "Kare wa moo kaetteru yo." | TF: Eng probe "He is on his way home right now." | Wrong ⇒ progressive/resultative collapse — the single most consequential -te iru error; makes shitteru, kiteru, motteru, wakatteru all misparse.
15 | -teru habitual | "Mainichi roku ji ni okiteru." | CQ: "Is he getting up right now?" | Wrong ⇒ only has the right-now reading; predicts misreading routine descriptions as live commentary.

16 | -chau completion | "Shukudai, yatchatta." | CQ: "Finished or not?" | Wrong ⇒ the -chau contraction is not lexicalized despite being the plan's citation form; a wk-9 curriculum failure, not a grammar failure.
17 | -chau regret / unintended | "Densha, norisugichatta." | CQ: "Did he mean to?" | Wrong ⇒ has the aspect but not the affect; will sound cold and will miss apology framing.
18 | -toku preparatory | "Biiru, hiyashitoku ne." | CQ: "Why is she doing it now?" | Wrong ⇒ -toku heard as -teru (they are close in fast speech); loses the whole in-advance meaning.

19 | -te aru (agentive result) vs -te iru (bare state) | "Kabe ni e ga kakete aru." / "Kabe ni e ga kakatte iru." | 2AFC: "Someone hung it on purpose" / "It's just there" | Wrong ⇒ agentivity of -te aru absent. Direct interference with B5.

20 | -te iku (away from deictic centre / progressive future) | "Kore kara dandan samuku natte iku." | CQ: "Getting colder or warmer? Now or over time?" | Wrong ⇒ deictic axis inverted; paired with 21.
21 | -te kuru (toward deictic centre / onset) | "Ame ga futte kita." | CQ: "When did it start?" | Wrong ⇒ same axis, opposite pole. 20/21 scored as a consistency pair; separate by >=25 items.
22 | -te miru trial | "Ichido tabete miru?" | CQ: "Is he asking you to look at it?" | Wrong ⇒ literal 'look' reading; a lexical trap that survives long past its frequency rank.

23 | -te mo concessive | "Ame ga futte mo iku yo." | TF: Eng probe "He'll go only if it doesn't rain." | Wrong ⇒ -te mo collapsed onto -tara; inverts the truth value of the sentence, the worst class of error.
blocks.rationale: Second-largest (11) on raw token frequency alone: -te auxiliaries are the highest-frequency productive machinery in spoken Japanese, and the plan's contraction-as-citation decision (-teru, -chau, -toku) means the exit test is also validating a curriculum bet. Error-proneness is moderate for the progressive but severe for resultative -teru, -te aru, and the iku/kuru deixis, none of which have English analogues. 11 items also buys enough coverage to tell a contraction-parsing failure (items 16, 18) apart from a semantics failure (14, 19, 20, 21) — a distinction the failure branch needs.
blocks.interference: Item 14 (resultative -teru) and item 48 (shimatteru, B5) test the same phenomenon on different verbs — keep >=30 apart and never let 48 come first. Item 19 (-te aru) must not be adjacent to items 44, 45, or 51 (B5) or the agentivity contrast gets primed. Item 20 shares change-of-state -ku naru with item 102 (B12); separate by >=20. Item 13 should be placed in the first five items of the session (anchor, warm-up).

blocks.label: B3. WA / GA — 10 items
items: 24 | ga for neutral description of a newly perceived event | "A, basu ga kita." | 2AFC audio: "basu ga kita" / "basu wa kita" against a picture of a bus arriving | Wrong ⇒ topic-marks new information; the most audible foreigner signature in production.
25 | wa contrastive | "Sakana wa taberu kedo, niku wa tabenai." | CQ: "What does he eat?" | Wrong ⇒ misses that the two wa are paired; predicts hearing a simple list.

26 | ga as exhaustive answer to a wh-question | Q: "Dare ga yatta no?" — 2AFC answers: "Boku ga yatta." / "Boku wa yatta." | 2AFC appropriateness | Wrong ⇒ THE diagnostic wa/ga error. Answering wh-questions with wa is the marker of a learner who has 'topic vs subject' as a slogan and not as a rule.

27 | wh-word cannot take wa | "Kore wa nan desu ka." vs "*Kore ga nan desu ka." | 2AFC aural naturalness — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY, non-gating | Wrong ⇒ the wh/particle alignment is not internalized; predicts item 26 failing too.

28 | ga with stative predicates (wakaru / dekiru / aru / hoshii) | "Nihongo ga wakaru?" vs "Nihongo o wakaru?" | 2AFC naturalness | Wrong ⇒ treats wakaru as transitive; the same defect will surface at item 88 (potential ga).

29 | Double-nominative possessor construction | "Zoo wa hana ga nagai." | CQ: "What is long?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot parse the wa...ga frame; will assign the predicate to the wrong noun in any description of body/parts/properties.

30 | ga inside a subordinate clause, wa in the main clause | "Watashi wa, kare ga kuru to omoimasu." | CQ: "Who is coming?" | Wrong ⇒ subject tracking dies at the clause boundary. This is a listening failure, not a particle failure, and predicts B19 failures.
31 | wa scoping over negation (partial negation) | "Zenbu wa tabenakatta." | TF: Eng probe "He ate nothing." | Wrong ⇒ misses partial negation; inverts a truth value. High cost, moderate frequency.

32 | Given/new tracking across two sentences | "Mukashi, ojiisan ga imashita. Ojiisan wa yama e ikimashita." | 2AFC for the SECOND sentence's particle | Wrong ⇒ no discourse-status tracking; the learner has wa/ga as a sentence-level rule only.
33 | mo occupying the wa/ga slot | "Watashi mo iku." vs "*Watashi wa mo iku." | 2AFC naturalness | Wrong ⇒ particle-slot competition unlearned; predicts stacking errors with wa/ga/o generally.
blocks.rationale: 10 items because wa/ga is simultaneously the highest-frequency decision in the language and the one with the longest documented error tail — learners who can state the rule still fail it at month 9 under speed. It gets fewer items than conditionals only because half its uses are recoverable from context in listening (the comprehension cost is lower than the production cost, and this battery gates listening). Items 26, 29, 30, 31 are the load-bearing four; 27 and 33 are cheap naturalness probes included because they cost little and separate 'knows the rule' from 'has the reflex'.
blocks.interference: Item 28 (ga with wakaru) and item 88 (ga with potential) are the same underlying phenomenon — place 28 early, 88 late, and score them as a linked pair for remediation purposes only. Item 30 primes B19 (items 133-137, ga inside modifier clauses); put all of B19 before item 30 or >=25 after it. Item 26's wh-question primes B17 (items 123-127) — separate by >=20.

blocks.label: B4. BENEFACTIVES (ageru / kureru / morau, bare and -te) — 10 items
items: 34 | ageru, outward direction from the speaker's sphere | "Imooto ni hon o katte ageta." | CQ: "Who ended up with the book?" | Wrong ⇒ direction inverted at the simplest level.
35 | kureru, obligatorily inward | "Tomodachi ga hon o katte kureta." | CQ: "Who paid?" | Wrong ⇒ the top benefactive error worldwide: ageru/kureru swap. Scored jointly with 34.

36 | kureru licensing a zero recipient | "Sensei ga oshiete kureta." | CQ: "Taught whom?" | Wrong ⇒ does not use kureru as the deictic cue that recovers the dropped 'me'; a direct listening cost in every conversation.
37 | morau, receiver as subject, agent in ni | "Tomodachi ni katte moratta." | CQ: "Who paid?" | Wrong ⇒ ni-agent under morau unparsed; the learner will invert who did the favour.

38 | kureru / morau as two framings of one event | "Kare ga tetsudatte kureta." then "Kare ni tetsudatte moratta." | TF: "Same event?" | Wrong ⇒ treats them as different events; means the system is memorized per-form, not understood as a perspective choice.

39 | ageru toward a superior is infelicitous | "Sensei ni nimotsu o motte agemashita." vs "Sensei no nimotsu o omochi shimashita." | 2AFC appropriateness — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ no politeness constraint on ageru; socially costly but not comprehension-costly, hence non-gating.

40 | kudasaru / itadaku upgrade | "Sensei ga oshiete kudasatta." | CQ: "Who taught, and is the speaker being deferential?" | Wrong ⇒ the honorific benefactive stems are unmapped; predicts total failure on service-encounter audio.

41 | -te kureru as a request, not an ability question | "Chotto matte kureru?" | CQ: "Is he asking whether you CAN wait, or asking you to wait?" | Wrong ⇒ conflates benefactive with potential; interference with B10.

42 | Negative benefactive question as softener | "Mado, akete kurenai?" vs "Mado, akete." | 2AFC: which is more polite | Wrong ⇒ the negative-as-softener principle is absent; generalizes to -masen ka, item 116.

43 | morau with a causative-ish reading of who acted | "Kodomo ni yasai o tabete moratta." | CQ: "Who ate the vegetables?" | Wrong ⇒ mis-assigns the actor under morau; the same defect reappears at item 106.
blocks.rationale: 10 items because the benefactive system is obligatory (omitting kureru is not merely less polite, it is ungrammatical-sounding), high-frequency in every service and favour exchange, and has zero English analogue — English 'give' does not encode deictic direction. Error persistence is extreme: learners routinely still fail ageru/kureru at year two. Weighted equal to wa/ga because the comprehension cost is higher: kureru is often the ONLY cue to who did what, since both arguments are dropped.
blocks.interference: Item 41 must be >=25 items from all of B10 (85-90) — it is a potential/benefactive homophony trap and priming either way corrupts both. Item 43 and item 106 (causative + morau) test overlapping structure; put 43 in the first half and 106 in the last quarter. Item 42 primes item 116 (-masen ka); separate by >=30. Items 34/35 adjacent is acceptable and intended (they form a direction pair), but 37 must not follow 35 within 10 items.

blocks.label: B5. TRANSITIVITY PAIRS — 9 items
items: 44 | akeru / aku | "Doa ga aita." vs "Doa o aketa." | 2AFC: "Did a person do it?" | Wrong ⇒ the pair system is not perceived at all; everything downstream in this block fails.

45 | tsukeru / tsuku, resultative | "Denki ga tsuite iru." | PIC 2AFC: room with light on, nobody present / person flipping the switch | Wrong ⇒ intransitive + resultative -teru read as an ongoing action; compound failure with item 14.

46 | kowasu / kowareru, blame assignment | "Keitai ga kowarechatta." | CQ: "Is he saying it's his fault?" | Wrong ⇒ assigns agency where Japanese explicitly declines to; predicts overusing the passive for accidents.
47 | otosu / ochiru, self-blame vs event | "Saifu, otoshita." vs "Saifu ga ochita." | CQ: "Who dropped it?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot report own error correctly; a daily-life failure.

48 | shimeru / shimaru + resultative | "Ano mise, moo shimatteru yo." | CQ: "Closed already, or closing now?" | Wrong ⇒ intransitive-plus-resultative compound; the highest-frequency real-world instance of this whole block.
49 | dasu / deru | "Gomi, dashita?" | CQ: "Who is supposed to have done what?" | Wrong ⇒ pair mismapped on a verb whose two members are semantically far apart in English ('take out' / 'leave').
50 | naosu / naoru with illness | "Kaze, naotta?" | CQ: "Did someone cure him, or did he get better?" | Wrong ⇒ applies the sick-person-as-agent frame; a small but very audible error.

51 | Intransitive+teiru vs PASSIVE+teiru | "Mado ga aite iru." vs "Mado ga akerarete iru." | 2AFC: "Did someone open it?" | Wrong ⇒ the deepest error in the block: the learner has collapsed the transitivity system into the passive because English renders both as 'is opened'. Highest information item here.

52 | hairu / ireru, containment frame | "Kaban ni saifu ga haitteru." | CQ: "Where is the wallet and did someone just put it there?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot do the location-state frame; blocks most 'where is my X' conversation.
blocks.rationale: 9 items. Frequency is very high (these are among the first 300 verbs) and error-proneness is high-and-persistent because English has no morphological pair system and translates both members identically. It sits below wa/ga and benefactives only because misparsing a pair usually costs agency information, not propositional content. Item 51 alone justifies two slots' worth of weight — the transitive/passive collapse is the failure mode that makes learners sound like they were taught by a translation engine.
blocks.interference: Item 51 is a passive item wearing a transitivity costume: it must be >=30 from all of B8 (70-77), and specifically must NOT follow item 75. Item 48 vs item 14 (resultative -teru) — >=30 apart, 14 first. Item 45 vs item 19 (-te aru) — >=20 apart. Item 46's -chau overlaps item 17; separate by >=15 or a -chau parsing failure double-counts.

blocks.label: B6. EVIDENTIALS (-soo appearance / soo da hearsay / rashii / mitai / yoo da) — 9 items
items: 53 | -soo appearance, i-adjective stem | "Kono keeki, oishisoo." | CQ: "Has he tasted it?" | Wrong ⇒ appearance/hearsay collapse. Scored jointly with 54.

54 | soo da hearsay, plain form attachment | "Kono keeki, oishii soo da yo." | CQ: identical probe wording to 53 | Wrong ⇒ same. The 53/54 pair isolates the attachment-site contrast (stem vs plain form) that is the ONLY formal difference — this is the most purely audio-testable evidential contrast in the language.
55 | -soo on a verb = imminence | "Ame ga furisoo." | CQ: "Is it raining?" | Wrong ⇒ imminent read as actual; inverts a factual claim.
56 | Irregular negative appearance stem (-nasasoo) | "Ano hito, genki ja nasasoo." | 2AFC form choice — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ morphological irregularity only; low comprehension cost, non-gating.

57 | rashii, secondhand report + typicality | "Kare, kekkon shita rashii yo." | CQ: "How does the speaker know?" | Wrong ⇒ rashii read as 'seems to me'; the learner has one undifferentiated evidential.
58 | mitai, inference from present direct evidence | "Dare mo inai mitai." | CQ: "Is the speaker looking at the place right now?" | Wrong ⇒ mitai/rashii source axis is flat.
59 | mitai simile (non-evidential) | "Mattaku kodomo mitai." | CQ: "Is he a child?" | Wrong ⇒ has only the evidential sense; will misparse a very common insult/joke frame.
60 | yoo da vs mitai register | Same proposition twice | 2AFC: which is more formal — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ register axis absent; non-gating because both are comprehensible.

61 | SOURCE TRIAGE under production pressure | Eng situation: "You smell smoke but see no fire. Say there seems to be a fire." | 4AFC audio: kaji rashii / kaji mitai / kaji da soo da / kaji ga okorisoo | Wrong ⇒ the whole evidential system is one word, 'seems'. Terminal item of the block.
blocks.rationale: 9 items because evidentials are grammatically obligatory in Japanese conversation (asserting hearsay as fact is a social error, not a stylistic one), extremely frequent in gossip/news-relay/plan talk, and English marks them only lexically and optionally — so the L1 gives no pressure to learn the distinction. Error-proneness is very high. Held to 9 rather than 12 because three of the five forms (mitai/yoo/rashii) overlap enough that even natives vary, so items past ~6 start measuring dialect rather than competence; slots 56 and 60 are therefore explicitly non-gating.
blocks.interference: 53/54 are the tightest minimal pair in the battery — separate by >=45 items (put 53 in block-order position ~15 of the administered sequence and 54 past position 100). 57 and 58 must be >=20 apart. Item 61 must be the LAST evidential item administered, since it reveals the contrast set. Item 55 (furisoo) shares the verb with item 21 (futte kita) — keep >=15 apart.

blocks.label: B7. REQUEST / PERMISSION / PROHIBITION PARADIGM — 8 items
items: 62 | -te kudasai | "Chotto matte kudasai." | CQ | ANCHOR ITEM, near-ceiling expected; a miss invalidates the session rather than scoring against the learner.
63 | -naide kudasai | "Koko de tabenaide kudasai." | CQ: "May he eat here?" | Wrong ⇒ the -nai stem + de is not formed; predicts producing 'tabanai de' or reverting to positive.

64 | -cha dame (contracted prohibition) | "Koko de tabecha dame." | CQ: "Allowed or not?" | Wrong ⇒ -cha contraction unparsed; since -cha is the plan's citation form this is a curriculum check as much as a grammar check.
65 | -te mo ii, permission request | "Kore, tabete mo ii?" | CQ: "Is he asking or telling?" | Wrong ⇒ permission frame absent.

66 | -nakute mo ii, EXEMPTION | "Muri shite konakute mo ii yo." | TF: Eng probe "You must not come." | Wrong ⇒ exemption read as prohibition. This is the most dangerous single confusion in the battery — it inverts a social obligation. Weight it double in remediation triage.
67 | -naide vs -nakute adverbial split | "Nenaide benkyoo shita." vs "Nemurenakute komatta." | 2AFC — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ manner-negative vs cause-negative not split; moderate cost, non-gating.

68 | Politeness gradient, three-way ORDERING | "Akete." / "Akete kurenai?" / "Akete itadakemasen ka." | Ordering task: rank three audio clips by politeness (no text, drag-free — spoken 1-2-3) | Wrong ⇒ no politeness scale; the learner will be either rude or absurdly formal with no middle.

69 | Prohibitive -na particle | "Iku na!" | CQ: "Go, or don't go?" | Wrong ⇒ hears the bare imperative and misses the single mora that negates it. Catastrophic in live use; short, fast, and easy to miss.
blocks.rationale: 8 items. Frequency is high and the paradigm is small and learnable, so error-proneness at month 9 SHOULD be low — which is exactly why 8 items are worth spending: this block is the battery's calibration floor. If items 62 and 65 are missed, the score is not measuring grammar. The extra weight beyond a bare paradigm sweep goes to items 64, 66, 69, which are the three where a single contracted or unstressed mora carries the whole polarity — pure audio-channel risk that a text test would never catch.
blocks.interference: Item 66 (-nakute mo ii) and item 81 (obligation 4AFC) test the same double-negative ladder from opposite ends — 66 must come well BEFORE 81 (>=15 apart) so that 81 measures the ladder rather than an echo. Item 64 and item 80 (-nakucha) are phonetically confusable in fast speech; separate by >=20. Item 62 belongs in the first five administered items alongside item 13.

blocks.label: B8. PASSIVE, THREE USES — 8 items
items: 70 | Direct passive, ni-marked agent | "Sensei ni homerareta." | CQ: "Who praised whom?" | Wrong ⇒ agent/patient inverted; the base failure.
71 | Direct passive with an o-marked body part | "Densha de ashi o fumareta." | CQ: "Whose foot, and who stepped?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot handle o under a passive; a construction English simply lacks.

72 | Indirect / adversative passive from an INTRANSITIVE | "Ame ni furareta." | CQ: "Is he pleased?" | Wrong ⇒ the adversative reading is missing entirely. The most-missed passive and the one with no English translation at all.
73 | Indirect passive, human agent | "Tonari no hito ni ban-juu sawagareta." | CQ: "Who was noisy, and who's complaining?" | Wrong ⇒ same axis as 72; scored as a consistency pair.
74 | Possessive-adversative passive | "Densha de saifu o nusumareta." | CQ: "Whose wallet?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot report being victimized — the highest-utility passive for a traveller.

75 | Non-agentive / descriptive passive | "Kono tatemono wa hyaku nen mae ni taterareta." | CQ: "Is the speaker complaining?" | Wrong ⇒ over-applies the adversative reading learned at 72-74; this item exists to catch overcorrection.

76 | Passive / potential homophony on ichidan | "Kono kinoko wa taberareru yo." with a disambiguating one-clause preamble | 2AFC: 'edible' / 'gets eaten by animals' | Wrong ⇒ homophony unresolved; the learner needs context to disambiguate and has not built that habit.

77 | Spontaneous -reru | "Mukashi no koto ga omoidasareru." | CQ: "Did he try to remember?" — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ spontaneous voice absent; genuinely low conversational frequency, so non-gating.
blocks.rationale: 8 items, split 2 direct / 3 indirect-adversative / 1 non-agentive / 1 homophony / 1 spontaneous. The allocation is deliberately skewed toward the adversative because that is where English gives zero support and where frequency in casual complaint-talk is highest; the direct passive is the one English speakers get for free and needs only two confirmatory items. Not larger than 8 because passive comprehension in listening is often recoverable from context, unlike conditionals where it is not.
blocks.interference: Item 76 is the passive/potential homophone and MUST be >=35 from every B10 item; ideally 76 is administered before B10 so the potential block does not prime the 'ability' reading. Item 75 must not be adjacent to item 51 (B5) — both probe 'did someone do it'. Items 72/73 are a pair; separate by >=15. Item 74 shares the 'saifu' lexeme with item 47 and item 52; use a different noun in one of them to prevent lexical priming.

blocks.label: B9. OBLIGATION LADDER — 7 items
items: 78 | -nakya (citation contraction) | "Yabai, moo ikanakya." | CQ: "Does he have to go or want to go?" | Wrong ⇒ the everyday obligation form is unparsed. Highest-frequency item in the block and the plan's designated citation form.
79 | -nakereba naranai (formal) | "Ashita made ni dasanakereba narimasen." | CQ: "By when, and is it optional?" | Wrong ⇒ formal-register obligation missing; matters for workplace/announcement audio.
80 | -nakucha (second contraction path) | "Moo sukoshi benkyoo shinakucha." | CQ | Wrong ⇒ only one of the two contractions was learned; predicts 50% miss rate on real obligation talk.

81 | LADDER SELECTION under production pressure | Eng situation: "Tell your friend they have to eat it." | 4AFC audio: tabenakya / tabenakute mo ii / tabecha dame / tabete mo ii | Wrong ⇒ the four rungs are undifferentiated; the single most informative item in the block. Direct interference with 64/65/66.

82 | -ta hoo ga ii (past form, non-past meaning) | "Kyoo wa yasunda hoo ga ii yo." | CQ: "Is he describing yesterday or giving advice?" | Wrong ⇒ reads -ta as tense; a form/function mismatch that persists for years.
83 | -nai hoo ga ii | "Ikanai hoo ga ii to omou." | CQ: "Should he go?" | Wrong ⇒ negative advice inverted; polarity error, high cost.
84 | beki, moral register | "Sonna koto iu beki ja nai." | CQ — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ register-marked and lower conversational load; non-gating.
blocks.rationale: 7 items. Frequency is high (obligation talk saturates daily conversation) and the ladder's rungs are polarity-inverting, so errors flip meaning rather than blur it. Held to 7 rather than 10 because four of the rungs share morphology with B7, so items there already carry part of the load — spending 10 here would double-count the same underlying -nai-stem competence. Item 81 is the load-bearing item; 78/80 exist specifically to check that the plan's contraction-first citation policy actually took.
blocks.interference: Item 81 must come >=15 after items 64, 65, and 66, and no B7 item may follow it. Items 78 and 80 are near-homophones in fast speech — >=20 apart. Item 82's -ta form interferes with item 137 (relative-clause tense) and item 2 (counterfactual -tara): keep 82 >=20 from both. Item 83 is a polarity item; do not place any other polarity item (66, 69, 121, 126) within 8 positions.

blocks.label: B10. POTENTIAL — 6 items
items: 85 | Godan potential off the e-stem | "Boku, zenzen oyogenai n da." | CQ: "Can't swim, or doesn't want to?" | Wrong ⇒ the wk-13 e-stem key failed to generalize; check jointly with item 4.
86 | Ichidan potential, full -rareru | "Asa hayaku okirareru?" | CQ | Wrong ⇒ ichidan potential unformed; the learner may be over-applying the godan pattern.

87 | ra-nuki colloquial potential | "Kore, mireru?" vs "Kore, mirareru?" | 2AFC: same meaning? — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ will not parse casual speech, which is a real listening cost, but the form is non-standard so it cannot gate.

88 | Potential argument marking (ga, not o) | "Nihongo ga hanaseru." vs "Nihongo o hanaseru." | 2AFC naturalness | Wrong ⇒ same defect as item 28; if both fail, remediate stative-ga as ONE lesson, not two.
89 | Suppletive potential: dekiru / suru-verbs | "Unten dekiru?" | CQ | Wrong ⇒ the most frequent potential in the language is not connected to the paradigm.

90 | Ability vs external permission | "Sumimasen, koko de wa taberaremasen." | CQ: "Is he saying you're incapable, or that it's not allowed?" | Wrong ⇒ conflates internal ability with situational permission; also a passive-homophony trap.
blocks.rationale: Only 6 items despite very high frequency, because the potential is morphologically regular, transparently glossable as 'can', and largely recoverable from context — error-proneness at month 9 should be LOW. Spending 10 here would buy little information. The six are chosen to isolate three distinct failure sources: stem formation (85, 86), argument marking (88), and semantic scope (90). Item 87 is included only because ra-nuki is ubiquitous in the casual audio this learner is training on, and its absence would silently cost comprehension.
blocks.interference: Entire block must be >=35 from item 76 (B8 passive homophone) and >=25 from item 41 (B4 -te kureru request). Item 88 pairs with item 28 — put 28 in the first third, 88 in the last third. Item 85 pairs with item 4 (both e-stem) — >=20 apart. Item 90 uses -raremasen which is formally identical to a passive; it must not be administered within 15 items of any B8 item.

blocks.label: B11. NOMINALIZERS (no / koto, incl. n da) — 6 items
items: 91 | no as obligatory complement of a perception verb | "Kare ga heya ni hairu no o mita." | CQ: "Saw what happen?" | Wrong ⇒ the no/koto selection rule for perception verbs is absent; also tests clause-internal ga (link to item 30).

92 | koto with an abstract/generic predicate | "Nihongo o hanasu koto wa muzukashii." | 2AFC no/koto — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ default nominalizer only; genuinely marginal in casual speech, so non-gating.

93 | n da / no da explanatory | "Atama ga itai n da." vs "Atama ga itai." | 2AFC: which one is offered as an EXPLANATION for something | Wrong ⇒ n da unparsed. Extremely frequent — arguably the highest-frequency single morpheme in this whole battery — and the plan makes -n da a citation form, so this is also a curriculum check.
94 | no as a pronominal head | "Motto akai no ga hoshii." | CQ: "What does she want?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot do headless ellipsis; blocks nearly all shopping and choosing talk.
95 | koto ga aru, experiential | "Nihon ni itta koto aru?" | CQ: "Ever, or right now?" | Wrong ⇒ experiential aspect read as a past event.

96 | koto ni suru vs koto ni naru, agentivity of a decision | "Raigetsu tenkin suru koto ni natta." | CQ: "Did he choose this?" | Wrong ⇒ inverts who decided; a socially loaded error in Japanese, which systematically de-agentivizes decisions.
blocks.rationale: 6 items. The no/koto contrast per se is over-taught relative to its conversational payoff — in casual speech no dominates and errors are rarely fatal, so it earns only two items (91, 92) and one of them is non-gating. The block's weight instead goes to the high-yield relatives: n da (93), pronominal no (94), and the two fixed frames (95, 96) that are effectively high-frequency vocabulary wearing grammar clothes. This is the clearest case in the allocation where textbook prominence and conversational value diverge.
blocks.interference: Item 91 contains a subordinate ga and primes items 30 and 135 — put 91 after both or >=25 apart. Item 93's n da appears incidentally in the stimulus of item 85; either strip it from 85 or keep them >=20 apart. Item 94's 'akai no' primes B12 adjective items; >=15 separation.

blocks.label: B12. ADJECTIVE INFLECTION — 6 items
items: 97 | i-adjective past | "Kinoo wa hontoo ni samukatta." | CQ: "Now or yesterday?" | Wrong ⇒ has not internalized that i-adjectives carry tense themselves; the #1 beginner adjective error and it persists.

98 | yokatta: suppletive stem + relief idiom | "Aa, yokatta." | CQ: "Is he saying something IS good, or that he's relieved about something that happened?" | Wrong ⇒ misses both the ii/yo- suppletion and the pragmatic relief function; yokatta is a top-50 conversational token.
99 | i-adjective negative -kunai | "Sonna ni takakunai yo." | CQ: "Expensive or not?" | Wrong ⇒ negative stem unformed; polarity error.

100 | na-adjective past/negative uses datta / ja nakatta | "Amari shizuka ja nakatta." vs "*shizukakunakatta" | 2AFC naturalness | Wrong ⇒ adjective class membership not stored per lexeme; the fix is lexical, not rule-based.
101 | Adverbial derivation by class (-ku vs -ni) | "Hayaku shite." / "Kirei ni shite." | 2AFC per class | Wrong ⇒ same class-membership defect as 100; if both fail, remediate as one problem.
102 | -ku naru / -ni naru change of state | "Kyuu ni samuku natte kita." | CQ: "Is it cold now, or getting colder?" | Wrong ⇒ change-of-state frame missing; compounds with item 20.
blocks.rationale: 6 items. Frequency is maximal but error-proneness at month 9 should be genuinely low for a learner who has carded 4,000+ items with adjectives inflected in audio — the forms are regular and highly repeated. So this block is a floor-check, not a probe, and 6 items suffice. The two slots that earn their keep beyond confirmation are 98 (yokatta's idiomatic relief use, which is opaque and frequent) and 100/101 (na-adjective class membership, which is lexical memory rather than rule and therefore never fully solved).
blocks.interference: Item 102 vs item 20 (-te iku change of state) — >=20 apart. Item 97 vs item 2 (-katta inside a counterfactual) — >=15. Item 99 is a polarity item; keep 8 positions clear of 66, 69, 83, 121, 126. Item 3 (yasukereba, B1) must not be adjacent to any item here.

blocks.label: B13. CAUSATIVE — 5 items
items: 103 | ni (let/permit) vs o (make/coerce) | "Kodomo ni ikaseta." vs "Kodomo o ikaseta." | 2AFC: 'let him go' / 'made him go' | Wrong ⇒ the causative's core semantic alternation is carried entirely by one particle; missing it means every causative is ambiguous. Highest-information item in the block.
104 | Godan causative formation | "Matasete gomen ne." | CQ: "Who was waiting?" | Wrong ⇒ -aseru not formed off the -nai stem; check jointly with item 63.

105 | Causative + kudasai = asking permission | "Kore, chotto yomasete kudasai." | CQ: "Who is going to read it?" | Wrong ⇒ the standard polite request-for-permission frame is unavailable; a high-utility everyday gap.
106 | Causative + morau (two-layer voice) | "Kyoo wa hayaku kaerasete moratta." | CQ: "Who gave permission, and who went home?" | Wrong ⇒ voice stacking fails; predicts item 140 failing.
107 | Causative of a psych verb | "Sensei o okorasechatta." | CQ: "Who got angry?" | Wrong ⇒ psych-causative argument structure inverted.
blocks.rationale: 5 items. The causative is frequent in workplace and family talk but is morphologically regular and — crucially — usually decodable from context, so error-proneness is moderate rather than severe. It also shares its stem with the negative (-nai stem, wk 8), so a failure here is usually a stem failure already detected elsewhere. Five items buy the one contrast that is NOT redundant (103's ni/o alternation) plus the two high-utility frames (105, 106) and one formation check.
blocks.interference: Item 106 vs item 43 (morau actor assignment) — >=20 apart, 43 first. The whole block must precede B20 (138-140) by >=10 but must NOT be adjacent to it, or the causative-passive items get scaffolded. Item 107's -chau overlaps items 16, 17, 46 — >=15 from each. Item 104 vs item 63 (-nai stem) — >=15.

blocks.label: B14. THE THREE -TTE — 5 items
items: 108 | Quotative tte (complementizer) | "Ashita kuru tte itteta yo." | CQ: "Who said it, and who's coming?" | Wrong ⇒ tte not recognized as a quote boundary; the learner will merge the quoted clause into the matrix and lose the speaker.
109 | Sentence-final hearsay tte | "Ashita, ame da tte." | CQ: "Does the speaker know this firsthand?" | Wrong ⇒ conflated with 108 and with soo da; scored jointly with item 54.
110 | Topic-marking / definitional tte (= wa / to iu no wa) | "Sore tte doo iu imi?" | CQ | Wrong ⇒ tte-as-wa unmapped; this is the most frequent of the three in casual speech.

111 | -te + tte adjacency (quoted request) | "'Chotto matte' tte itta yo." | CQ: "What were the exact words?" | Wrong ⇒ cannot segment two identical-sounding morae with different functions; a genuine audio-channel parsing trap that no written test would catch.
112 | tte vs to as register variants | "Kuru to omou." vs "Kuru tte omou." | 2AFC naturalness — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ register mapping only; non-gating.
blocks.rationale: 5 items — one per function plus the adjacency trap plus one non-gating register probe. The three -tte are individually very frequent but they are disambiguated almost entirely by POSITION (clause-internal, sentence-final, post-nominal), which is a cheap and robust cue, so error-proneness after 9 months of audio should be moderate. Item 111 is the reason this block exists at all as an AUDIO battery: the -te/-tte sequence is the clearest case where the difficulty is acoustic segmentation rather than syntax, and it is invisible to a text test.
blocks.interference: Item 109 vs item 54 (soo da hearsay) — >=25 apart; they test the same evidential function through different morphology and a correct answer on one strongly predicts the other. Item 108 and 111 both involve quoted speech — >=15 apart, with 108 first (111 is the harder segmentation). Item 110's 'doo iu' primes B17 question words — >=15.

blocks.label: B15. VOLITIONAL — 5 items
items: 113 | -oo as invitation | "Sorosoro ikoo ka." — use "Issho ni ikoo." | CQ: "Is he inviting you or predicting?" | Wrong ⇒ volitional form not distinguished from plain non-past in fast speech.
114 | -oo ka as an offer | "Mado, akeyoo ka?" | CQ: "Is he offering to open it, or asking your permission to?" | Wrong ⇒ the offer function is missing; the learner will hear a request instead.

115 | -oo to omou / -oo to omotteru, intention | "Rainen Nihon ni ikoo to omotteru." | CQ: "Decided, or still considering?" | Wrong ⇒ intention read as a firm plan; a nuance error with real social consequences.
116 | -mashoo vs -masen ka as invitations | Two clips, same content | 2AFC: which is the softer invitation | Wrong ⇒ the negative-question softener principle is absent; generalizes from item 42.

117 | Volitional formation across all three classes | Eng cues: 'let's drink / let's eat / let's do it' | PROD, native-reference match: nomoo / tabeyoo / shiyoo | Wrong ⇒ class-conditioned volitional not automatic; scored as ONE item requiring all three.
blocks.rationale: 5 items. Frequency is high but the volitional is formally regular, semantically transparent to English speakers ('let's / I think I'll'), and mostly recoverable from context — error-proneness is low. The allocation therefore buys the two functions English does NOT map cleanly (114's offer reading and 115's tentative intention) plus one formation check, and nothing more. Spending 8 here would be measuring something already solved.
blocks.interference: Item 116 vs item 42 (negative-question softener) — >=30 apart; they test the identical pragmatic principle and adjacency would make the second item free. Item 117 (PROD) should not be adjacent to any other PROD item (4, 124, 131) — cluster no more than one production item per 15 positions to control speaking-mode warm-up effects.

blocks.label: B16. COMPARISON — 5 items
items: 118 | yori / no hoo ga | "Densha yori basu no hoo ga yasui yo." | CQ: "Which is cheaper?" | Wrong ⇒ comparison direction inverted; a bare propositional error.
119 | dochira no hoo ga question frame | "Neko to inu to, dochira no hoo ga suki?" | CQ / PROD short answer | Wrong ⇒ cannot field the standard comparative question, which is a staple of small talk.
120 | ichiban superlative | "Kono naka de kore ga ichiban takai." | CQ | Wrong ⇒ superlative frame absent; low difficulty, included as a floor check.

121 | hodo ~nai (negative comparison) | "Kyoo wa kinoo hodo samukunai." | TF: Eng probe "Today is colder than yesterday." | Wrong ⇒ the trap item of the block: hodo+negative inverts, and the surface order looks like a positive comparison to an English ear.
122 | to onaji kurai (equative) | "Boku to onaji kurai no se da yo." | CQ: "Taller, shorter, or the same?" | Wrong ⇒ equative frame missing; forces a binary reading onto a three-way scale.
blocks.rationale: 5 items. Comparison is frequent but structurally simple and heavily lexicalized (yori, hoo, ichiban are effectively vocabulary), so error-proneness at month 9 is low. Four of the five items are floor checks; item 121 is the only one with genuine information value, because hodo+negative is the one comparison structure whose surface order misleads an English listener. Allocating more would be paying for confirmation.
blocks.interference: Item 121 is a polarity item; keep 8 positions clear of items 66, 69, 83, 99, 126. Item 119 primes B17 (dochira is a question word) — >=15 from items 123-127. Item 118 and 121 both use temperature/price scales; vary the lexical field so a vocabulary gap does not masquerade as a grammar gap.

blocks.label: B17. QUESTION WORDS AND THE KA/MO/DEMO SERIES — 5 items
items: 123 | Core wh inventory | Five short clips: "Dare?" / "Nani ga?" / "Doko de?" / "Itsu?" / "Ikura?" in minimal carrier sentences | CQ each; scored as ONE item, credit only if 5/5 | ANCHOR ITEM — near-ceiling expected. A miss invalidates the session.

124 | dooshite / nande + reason answer | "Nande kinoo konakatta no?" | PROD: give a one-clause reason ending in kara | Wrong ⇒ cannot field reason questions, which are the engine of any real conversation.

125 | ka-series indefinites (dareka / nanika / dokoka) | "Sakki dareka kita?" | CQ: "Is he asking WHO came, or WHETHER anyone came?" | Wrong ⇒ the ka-series is collapsed onto the bare wh-word; the learner will answer the wrong question, constantly.
126 | mo-series with obligatory negative (daremo / nanimo) | "Kesa wa nanimo tabenakatta." | TF: Eng probe "He ate something this morning." | Wrong ⇒ negative concord not built; inverts truth value.
127 | demo-series, free choice | "Nandemo ii yo, makaseru." | CQ: "Does he have a preference?" | Wrong ⇒ demo-series missing; will read indifference as a specific request.
blocks.rationale: 5 items, and note that only ONE of them (123) covers the bare question words — that is deliberate. Bare wh-words are among the earliest and most repeated items in any audio curriculum; testing them heavily would waste slots on a solved problem. The real error mass sits in the ka/mo/demo derivational series (125, 126, 127), which are high-frequency, minimally different acoustically (dareka / daremo / daredemo), and systematically confused. Three of five slots go there.
blocks.interference: Item 123 belongs in the first five administered items (anchor/warm-up) alongside items 13 and 62. Items 125/126/127 are a three-way morphological series — space them >=12 apart from each other so the series structure is not revealed. Item 126 is a polarity item: 8 clear positions from 66, 69, 83, 99, 121. Item 26 (ga answering a wh-question) must be >=20 from 123.

blocks.label: B18. COUNTERS AND NUMBERS — 5 items
items: 128 | Counter class selection | Picture of three pens | 4AFC audio: sanmai / sanbon [1, approximate] / sanko / sannin | Wrong ⇒ counter class not bound to object shape; a production error mainly, hence one slot only.

129 | Accent-borne minimal pair on a counter | "Biiru, nihon [1] onegai." vs "Nihon [3, approximate] no biiru." | 2AFC by ACCENT ALONE, no segmental difference | Wrong ⇒ the accent integer carried on every card was decorative, not perceptual. This is the battery's only direct audit of the plan's accent policy, and it is worth a slot for that reason alone.

130 | Irregular readings in time/date | Four clips: "yoji" / "kuji" / "shichiji" / "hatsuka" in carrier sentences | CQ each, scored as ONE item, credit at 4/4 | Wrong ⇒ irregular readings not memorized; pure listening, no grammar involved, but a total blocker for scheduling talk.

131 | Myriad-based grouping (man scale) | "Zenbu de ichi man go sen en desu." | PROD: say the amount in English digits | Wrong ⇒ cannot convert at the 10,000 boundary — a near-universal English-speaker failure that survives fluency in everything else.
132 | Quantifier float position | "Biiru o sanbon kudasai." vs "Sanbon no biiru o kudasai." | 2AFC naturalness — DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY | Wrong ⇒ quantifier placement; production-side only, non-gating.
blocks.rationale: 5 items, and this block is included under protest: counters and numbers are only marginally grammar. They earn slots because (a) item 131 is a hard listening blocker with a documented near-universal failure rate among English speakers regardless of overall level, and (b) item 129 is the ONLY place in the whole battery where pitch accent is put on trial, which the plan's every-card-carries-an-accent-integer policy obliges. The other three are cheap floor checks. If the battery had to shrink, this block gives up items 128 and 132 first.
blocks.interference: Item 129 is an accent item and must not be adjacent to any other item where accent could be a confound; place it in an otherwise segmentally easy stretch. Item 132 uses sanbon like 128 — >=15 apart. Item 131 is a PROD item: keep >=15 from items 4, 117, 124. NOTE: accent integers here are marked APPROXIMATE and must be verified against a standard-Tokyo accent dictionary before recording; if 129's pair cannot be recorded cleanly by a single Tokyo speaker, cut the item rather than record an unreliable contrast.

blocks.label: B19. NOUN-MODIFYING (RELATIVE) CLAUSES — 5 items
items: 133 | Subject-gap modifier | "Kinoo kita hito, dare datta?" | CQ: "Who did what?" | Wrong ⇒ the prenominal clause boundary is not heard; the learner is parsing left-to-right with English expectations and will lose the head noun.
134 | Object-gap modifier | "Kinoo katta hon, doko ni oita?" | CQ | Wrong ⇒ gap role misassigned; will think the book bought something.

135 | ga-marked subject INSIDE the modifier | "Watashi ga tsukutta ryoori, doo datta?" | CQ: "Who cooked?" | Wrong ⇒ reads the embedded ga as the main-clause subject; this is the same defect as item 30 and is the practical reason learners lose the thread in fast speech.

136 | Non-gap (appositive) modification | "Tomodachi ga kekkon suru hanashi, kiita?" | CQ: "What is the news about?" | Wrong ⇒ forces a gap reading onto a clause that has none; a structure English lacks entirely.

137 | Relative tense is relative to the main clause | "Ashita kuru hito" vs "Kinoo kita hito" in past-tense matrix sentences | 2AFC time reference | Wrong ⇒ imports English sequence-of-tense; will misdate every embedded event.
blocks.rationale: 5 items, which understates the construction's frequency (noun modification is everywhere) and overstates the learner's likely competence — this is the block where I am least confident the allocation is right. The justification: relative-clause comprehension failures show up as failures on OTHER items (30, 91) and so are partly measured already, and by month 9 an audio-first learner has heard tens of thousands of prenominal modifiers. The five items isolate the four structurally distinct cases plus the tense rule. If the failure branch shows misses concentrated here, treat it as a parsing-speed signature rather than a knowledge gap.
blocks.interference: Item 135 vs item 30 vs item 91 all test embedded ga — space all three >=25 apart and administer 133/134 before any of them. Item 137's -ta form interferes with item 82 (-ta hoo ga ii) — >=20. Item 136 uses 'hanashi' as a non-gap head; do not reuse that noun anywhere else in the battery.

blocks.label: B20. CAUSATIVE-PASSIVE — 3 items
items: 138 | Godan causative-passive contraction (-sareru) | "Nomasareta yo, mata." | CQ: "Did he want to drink?" | Wrong ⇒ the contracted -sareru is unparsed; this is the form that actually occurs in speech, so it outranks the full form.

139 | Ichidan causative-passive, full form | "Kodomo no koro, mainichi yasai o tabesaserareta." | CQ: "Who is unhappy about it?" | Wrong ⇒ the full stack is not decomposed; the learner hears a long verb and gives up.

140 | THREE-WAY VOICE DISCRIMINATION | Eng situation: "Your boss made you stay late and you resented it. Say so." | 3AFC audio: nokorasareta / nokorasareru... — nokosareta (passive) / nokoraseta (causative) / nokorasareta (causative-passive) | Wrong ⇒ the voice stack has collapsed. TERMINAL ITEM: deliberately the hardest in the battery, placed last, and expected to be missed by a majority of passing learners.
blocks.rationale: 3 items — the smallest block, and the clearest example of the allocation refusing to be even. The causative-passive is morphologically the most complex form in the closed set and it is the one every syllabus treats as a capstone, but its conversational token frequency is low (it clusters in complaint narratives) and its meaning is almost always recoverable from context and prosody. Three items confirm whether the form is parsed at all; nothing beyond that is worth a slot. Note that 140 is expected to be missed by many passing learners and its miss should NOT trigger remediation on its own.
blocks.interference: Must be the final three items administered, and >=10 after all of B13 (causative) and >=10 after all of B8 (passive) — the whole point is that the learner reaches them without recent scaffolding. Items 138 and 139 must not be adjacent (different classes, same stack). Item 140's three options are near-homophones; record them with a single speaker at identical rate, and pilot the contrast on native listeners before use — if natives are below 95% on the 3AFC, the item is a recording problem, not a learner problem.

notes: FORMAT TAXONOMY (answers requirement 4). Every item is delivered as audio; the learner never sees Japanese in any script. Carrier prompts and probes are in spoken ENGLISH, which is legitimate because the learner is an English speaker and the test measures Japanese comprehension, not instruction-following. Codes used above: CQ = content question (hear Japanese, answer a spoken English question about who/what/when — no metalanguage, no grammar terms); TF = truth-value judgment (hear Japanese, then hear an English paraphrase, say same/different — the strongest format available, because a wrong grammatical parse flips the answer); 2AFC/3AFC/4AFC = forced choice between audio candidates given a spoken English situation; PIC = picture forced choice (images are not text, so this is available and is the only clean way to test resultative states and counters); PROD = spoken production scored against a native reference plus a pre-written acceptance list of alternates; SEQ = event-ordering probe; GJ = aural naturalness judgment. Distribution: CQ 71, 2AFC/3AFC/4AFC 46, TF 8, PROD 5, PIC 2, SEQ 2, ordering 1, plus 5 multi-clip composites.

WHAT CANNOT BE TESTED WITHOUT TEXT, HONESTLY. Three things. (1) Ungrammaticality judgments. Items 6 (-to main-clause constraint), 27 (wh-word cannot take wa), 33 (mo in the wa/ga slot), 39 (ageru upward), 67 (-naide vs -nakute), 92 (koto), 100 (na-adj), 112 (tte vs to), 132 (quantifier float) all require the learner to reject a form. In audio this becomes 'which of these two sounds like something a Japanese person would say', which is contaminated by prosody, by voice quality, and by the learner's willingness to guess. WORKAROUND ADOPTED: all nine are marked DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY and excluded from the gating score (see power note). They are administered because they are cheap and their pattern is informative for remediation, but they never fail anyone. (2) Morphological form-production in isolation. Items 4, 117, 131 use PROD with a native-reference acceptance list rather than a written blank; this works but requires a human or forced-alignment scorer, which is the battery's only non-automatable cost. Budget for it. (3) Register contrasts (60, 112) where both forms are grammatical and the difference is formality. These are the weakest items in the battery; they survive only as diagnostics.

STATISTICAL POWER, STATED PROPERLY (answers requirement 5). The plan's 18/20 and 16/20 sub-battery gates are not usable: at n=20 and p=0.9 the binomial SD is 1.34 items, i.e. +/-6.7 percentage points per SD, so an 18/20 cut cannot separate a true-90% learner from a true-78% learner at any acceptable error rate. Discard them. At n=140 and p=0.9 the SD is 3.55 items (2.5pp), which is workable — BUT items are clustered in 20 blocks averaging 7 items, and within-block responses are correlated (a learner who fails one conditional tends to fail others). At a conservative intra-cluster correlation of 0.15, the design effect is 1 + (7-1)(0.15) = 1.9, giving an effective n of about 74 and an effective SD of about 4.9 items on the 140 scale. Consequence: the raw cut must NOT be set at the nominal 126/140. At a 126 cut, a learner whose true ability is exactly 90% passes only about half the time. RECOMMENDED CUT: 122/140 raw (87.1%), applied to the 131 gating items only (see next note) — this gives a true-90% learner roughly an 82-85% chance of passing and a true-80% learner roughly a 3% chance. Report the nominal standard as 'about 90%' and implement it as 122. The grey band 116-121 is genuinely unresolvable and should trigger a retest on parallel form B, not a decision.

WHICH SUB-SCORES GATE AND WHICH DO NOT. GATING: the overall score across the 131 non-diagnostic items, cut at 122. SECONDARY GATE (advisory, may delay but not fail): the 'structural core' composite of B1+B2+B3+B4 = 43 items, SD about 4.6pp, cut at 36/43 — this is the smallest aggregate in the battery with defensible power, and it is the one worth watching because those four blocks are where a real knowledge deficit shows first. EVERYTHING ELSE IS DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY. No individual block of 12 or fewer items can gate: at n=12 and p=0.9 the SD is 8.7pp, at n=6 it is 12pp, at n=3 it is 17pp. Block scores are for routing remediation, nothing more. Anyone quoting 'he got 4/6 on potential' as a decision input is reading noise. The 9 diagnostic-only items excluded from the gate are 6, 27, 39, 56, 60, 67, 77, 84, 92, 112, 132 — that is 11 items, so the gating set is 129, not 131; recount before use and adjust the cut proportionally (122/131 -> 120/129, 93.0%... no: hold the cut at 87% of the gating set, i.e. 112/129). USE 112/129 AS THE OPERATIONAL CUT. The three anchor items (13, 62, 123) are inside the gating set but a miss on any of them voids the session rather than scoring against the learner.

PARALLEL FORMS ARE MANDATORY, NOT OPTIONAL. Because the failure branch requires a retest, 280 items must be written, not 140 — form A and form B, matched item-for-item on construction, format, stimulus length in morae, and speaking rate, differing only in lexical content drawn from the learner's carded vocabulary. Retesting on form A measures memory of form A. Building form B roughly doubles the authoring cost of this battery and it must be budgeted at the same time, not deferred.

THE REPLAY DIAGNOSTIC — the mechanism that makes the failure branch decidable. The plan asserts that failure usually means speed, not knowledge, but as written the battery cannot tell those apart, so the assertion is untestable. FIX: immediately after scoring, re-administer ONLY the missed items under two relaxations — unlimited replays and a 0.8x time-stretched track (pitch-preserved, not pitch-shifted). Recovery rate R = (items recovered) / (items missed). R >= 0.70 = speed-dominant. R <= 0.40 = knowledge-dominant. 0.40 < R < 0.70 = mixed. This costs about 20 extra minutes and converts the plan's assumption into a measurement. Secondary signature: if misses are spread across >=10 blocks with no block below 60%, treat as speed-dominant even at middling R; if >50% of misses fall in <=3 blocks, treat as knowledge-dominant even at high R.

FAILURE BRANCH AT 78% (answers requirement 6). 78% is about 101/129 gating items, roughly 28 misses — that is about 4 SD below the cut, so it is a real deficit, not sampling noise. No retest is warranted; branch immediately on R. SPEED-DOMINANT (R >= 0.70): grammar still closes at month 9 as the hard ceiling requires. The reorder is to the DAILY LOOP, not the curriculum. (a) Retire every slow or over-articulated TTS voice from the review stream permanently; all reviews at 1.0x, with 20% of reviews at 1.15x. (b) Insert a 300-item reduction-and-contraction block into the ordinary card stream at 5/day for 60 days, displacing new vocabulary: n desu > n da > nda, -te iru > -teru > -ten, dewa > ja, -te shimau > -chau > -chatta, sore de wa > sorya, to iu > ttsu / tte, -nakereba > -nakya, no > n, ga > sentence-final drop, and the high-frequency vowel devoicings. These are cards, not lessons. (c) Add 10 min/day of shadowing on already-known material. (d) Keep the new-card rate at 20/day; do not reduce it. Retest on form B at month 10. If still below cut with the same speed signature, DO NOT extend grammar — proceed to vocabulary-only and let listening hours close the gap; the ceiling is the ceiling.

FAILURE BRANCH, KNOWLEDGE-DOMINANT (R <= 0.40) AND MIXED. KNOWLEDGE-DOMINANT: the month-9 ceiling still holds — grammar STUDY stops — but the failed constructions convert into ordinary cards rather than remaining as 'grammar work'. Rank the failed blocks by their allocation weight above (the weight IS the remediation priority; that is a second use for the same ordering variable). The top three failed blocks get 10 carded exemplars each in FIXED LEXICAL FRAMES — not paradigm drill, not conjugation tables: 10 different sentences containing 'ittara', not 10 verbs conjugated into -tara. Insert at 4/day inside the existing 20/day cap, displacing new vocabulary. That caps the intrusion at 20% of throughput for about 8 weeks and pushes the 6,000-word date from month 12-13 to roughly month 13-14. Retest only the failed blocks at month 11, as a diagnostic, never as a gate — remember no single block has the power to gate. MIXED (0.40 < R < 0.70): run both, but cap the vocabulary displacement at 2/day for remediation cards plus 3/day for reduction cards, total 5/day, same 20/day ceiling.

WHAT SURPRISED ME IN DOING THIS ALLOCATION. (1) The categories the syllabus treats as capstones — causative-passive, passive spontaneous, no vs koto — deserve the FEWEST items, because their conversational frequency is low and their meaning is context-recoverable. Difficulty is not the same as information value. (2) Three categories are really vocabulary wearing grammar clothes: koto ga aru, hoo ga ii, ichiban. They are tested here for completeness but a failure on them is a vocabulary failure and should be remediated as one. (3) The single highest-information item in the whole battery is probably item 51 (mado ga aite iru vs akerarete iru), because it simultaneously tests transitivity, resultative aspect, and passive, and English collapses all three. If only one item survived, that would be it. (4) Item 129 is the only place the plan's every-card-carries-an-accent-integer policy is ever audited. That is an uncomfortable ratio: a policy applied to 6,000 cards, tested by one item. Either add three more accent-contrast items (taking B18 to 8 and trimming B16 to 2), or accept openly that accent is being carried for production benefit and is not being validated by this test at all.

APPROXIMATIONS FLAGGED. Accent integers in items 128 and 129 (ippon, nihon 'two cylinders' vs Nihon 'Japan', sanbon) are given from memory and marked APPROXIMATE; verify against a standard-Tokyo accent dictionary before recording, and cut item 129 rather than record an unreliable contrast. The intra-cluster correlation of 0.15 used in the design-effect calculation is an assumption, not a measurement — recompute it from the first 20 administrations and re-derive the cut. The claim that a true-90% learner passes at 82-85% under the 87% cut depends on that ICC; if the real ICC is 0.30 the effective n drops to about 51 and the cut should move to 84-85% of the gating set.
orderingVariable: EXPECTED ERROR MASS at month 9, defined as the product of three factors per construction: (a) token frequency in conversational Japanese (CEJC-like spoken corpora, not written, not CSJ), x (b) estimated probability the learner is still wrong on it at month 9 given an audio-only curriculum with English as L1, x (c) comprehension cost of being wrong — where "inverts a truth value or an agent" scores maximum and "sounds slightly off" scores near zero. That product, normalized, allocates the 140 slots. Blocks are laid out in strictly descending order of the product, from 12 items (conditionals) down to 3 (causative-passive). Within each block, items run from the highest-frequency/lowest-processing-load exemplar to the highest-load discrimination, so that a partial-credit pattern within a block reads directly as a depth-of-mastery gradient. NOTE: this is the LAYOUT order, not the ADMINISTRATION order — administration is a constrained randomization that honors the separation requirements recorded in each block's interference field.
whyThatVariable: The obvious alternative is even allocation across the sixteen-to-twenty named categories — roughly 7-9 items each — which is what "the closed set has sixteen categories" implicitly proposes. Even allocation is wrong because it spends the same measurement budget on causative-passive (morphologically hard, conversationally rare, context-recoverable) as on the four conditionals (four overlapping forms, one syntactic constraint, one ordering contrast, all invisible in English translation, all high-frequency). A test's job is to reduce uncertainty about the pass/fail decision, and uncertainty lives where frequency and error-proneness overlap — not where difficulty alone is highest. The second obvious alternative is ordering by pedagogical difficulty or JLPT level, which is worse still: it correlates with textbook prominence rather than with what the learner will actually mis-hear, and it would put causative-passive at 12 items and wa/ga at 3. The third factor (comprehension cost) is included because this battery gates LISTENING, not production: a learner who says "sensei ni motte agemashita" is rude but understood, while a learner who hears "konakute mo ii" as "you must not come" has inverted the message. Rudeness gets diagnostic-only items; inversion gets gating items. Finally, the same ordering variable is reused downstream: the block weights are the remediation priority order in the failure branch, so one number does two jobs and there is no second, inconsistent ranking to maintain.
